title: 3 Training Camp Notes from Day 3 of 49ers practice: What’s Deebo Samuel up to?
summary: What would a training camp be for the San Francisco 49ers without a soul-crushing injury update? For the most part, the 49ers were healthy coming into camp. Even the players on the PUP list were not considered a big deal, with returns on the horizon for all four players. Fast forward to the day after […]
full_text: What would a training camp be for the San Francisco 49ers without a soul-crushing injury update? For the most part, the 49ers were healthy coming into camp. Even the players on the PUP list were not considered a big deal, with returns on the horizon for all four players. Fast forward to the day after day three of open practices, and there is a huge amount of concern. Let’s run down three notes from day three of training camp for the 49ers. Ricky Pearsall’s knee swelling is a cause for major concern Pearsall dealt with a PCL issue in his knee last season, but the thought was that an offseason of rest would rectify the issue. Well, here we are with swelling in the same knee, and the team announced there is concern and “everything is on the table.” That means it could just be a wait-and-see approach for Pearsall to see if the swelling goes down, or he could opt for surgery to repair the PCL. This isn’t a simple answer either. If they opt for a wait-and-see approach, then a plan to monitor the issue and his practice time has to be in place. If surgery is the move, that will end his season. Matt Maiocco went on KNBR and explained the timeline and the possibility of Pearsall missing the season. In the meantime, this is a golden opportunity for rookie wide receiver D’Zhaun Stribling to take command of a role. Anyone know what Deebo Samuel is up to these days? D’Zhaun Stribling continues to impress Opportunity pops up for players very quickly. Before the news of Pearsall’s injury, Stribling was already turning heads. The difference now is that Stribling is in line for a large role in the offense, as opposed to a role similar to Jauan Jennings in 2023. ESPN’s Nick Wagoner envisions Stribling’s role in the offense and where he would line up. “Rookie De’Zhaun Stribling was already making a positive first impression, and that continued on Wednesday. He’s fast but has a smooth speed that seems to allow him to accelerate and decelerate with little issue. He’s also big enough and unafraid to go over the middle. Had him down for five more catches Wednesday, including a nice job climbing the ladder on a high pass over the middle from Adrian Martinez. It’s hard to say how things will shake out in terms of alignment, but Stribling is working all three spots right now. My early guess: If Pearsall misses time, they’d like to go with Kirk or Demarcus Robinson at ‘Z’ and let Stribling handle the ‘Y.’” Jack Jones isn’t going quietly from the CB2 battle The 49ers signed Jones in the offseason with a reputation for being a ball hawk and someone who creates turnovers. Also, to send a message to Renardo Green. Green has turned heads under Raheem Morris so far, but Jones continues to put pressure on the young cornerback. Jones intercepted another pass on Wednesday intended for Jacob Cowing. Jones is a feast-or-famine type cornerback, but it is nice to know the 49ers have some semblance of reliable depth in the secondary. Green is still the frontrunner for the job, but Jones isn’t making that decision easy. That is a good thing.
author: Jason Aponte

title: 49ers insider says not to expect Ricky Pearsall to make any contributions in 2026
summary: When the news came out that San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Ricky Pearsall had knee swelling that concerned the team, it was easy for fans to think of the worst-case scenario immediately. How could you not with the way Pearsall’s career has started? He was shot in San Francisco as a rookie in an attempted […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - JANUARY 17: Ricky Pearsall #1 of the San Francisco 49ers stands on the sidelines during the national anthem prior to an NFL divisional playoff football game against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on January 17, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images When the news came out that San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Ricky Pearsall had knee swelling that concerned the team, it was easy for fans to think of the worst-case scenario immediately. How could you not with the way Pearsall’s career has started? He was shot in San Francisco as a rookie in an attempted robbery . After starting out hot in the first month of the season, a PCL injury sidelined Pearsall for nearly two months. He didn’t recapture that early-season mojo until December before re-aggravating the injury . According to Matt Maiocco, the latest on Pearsall “doesn’t look good” in an interview on KNBR : The PCL is an injury that oftentimes heals on its own. And that was the expectation last year. He injured that thing, came back, kinda re-aggravated it, and he had a difficult time shaking that. Well, the idea was, or the thought, was that it would heal on its own through the offseason. It doesn’t appear as if that has happened. After the first two days of training camp, which he ran all of the routes. He wasn’t limited in any fashion. He experienced swelling in that knee. And now, it’s kind of back to the drawing board. If surgery is required, he’s going to miss the season. He’s going to miss the entire season. And I know, even looking at it objectively, you’re like, ‘Gosh, this happened the second day of training camp,’ where the swelling became so bad that they had to back him off and kind of seek medical advice to determine what they’re going to do. The idea and the reason the 49ers didn’t kind of push the envelope and have him experience the surgery early in the offseason is because the expectation was that it could heal on its own. And if they decided to have the surgery, say in February or March, or whenever, you’re not giving it the full time to recover on its own. But, probably, you’re going to miss the season anyway. So, I think they made a calculated attempt to hope, I guess, that that thing would heal on its own. And once it didn’t, now it’s time for the 49ers and Ricky Pearsall to decide what they want to do. Now, I guess if you have that surgery, you’ve got to look ahead. This is his third year in the NFL. If they wait and wait and wait, and try to play through it, maybe the srugery is required. Maybe that cuts into his 2027 season. At this point, I think it’s reasonable, rational, logical, for the 49ers to not expect Ricky Pearsall to make any contribution in 2026. So, really kind of amplifies how important it was for the team to select De’Zhaun Stribling where they did with the 33rd overall pick. At the time, many people thought it was kind of a luxury pick. But now, it’s looking more and more like a necessity. It would be difficult to script a worse way for Pearsall’s career to begin if he needs surgery. Pearsall is a high-quality wide receiver who raises the ceiling of the offense. Stribling could be eased in if Pearsall was in the lineup. Teams would theoretically load up on Mike Evans and make a rookie beat them without Pearsall in the fold. You hope that there is a way for Pearsall to play through the pain and stay on the field in 2026, but the more information that comes out, the less likely it feels that’ll be the case.
author: Kyle Posey

title: Klay Kubiak shares the benefits of the 49ers changing up their practice schedule
summary: For several years under Kyle Shanahan, the San Francisco 49ers typically practiced three days in a row. The team changed their schedule for this training camp. It’s technically the first week, and the 49ers practiced Sunday and Monday before having a “jog-thru” on Tuesday. They returned to the practice field on Wednesday and were given […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - MAY 28: Head coach Mike Shanahan (L) and offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak (R) of the San Francisco 49ers talk during a team OTA practice at SAP Performance Facility on May 28, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images For several years under Kyle Shanahan, the San Francisco 49ers typically practiced three days in a row. The team changed their schedule for this training camp. It’s technically the first week, and the 49ers practiced Sunday and Monday before having a “jog-thru” on Tuesday. They returned to the practice field on Wednesday and were given Thursday off. Offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak was asked whether this change was due to the number of injuries the 49ers suffered at wide receiver last summer, in an effort to keep everyone, specifically the receivers, fresh and healthy throughout the summer. It’s a fair question, with injuries to Jauan Jennings, Jacob Cowing, and Jordan Watkins. But Kubiak and the 49ers — or any team — aren’t going to change their schedule to benefit one position group. Kubiak said, “It’s definitely not just about the receivers. We’re never going to make an adjustment to benefit one position group. It was a team thing. Just studying, talking to different people around the league and looking at different ways people do camp. We just thought it was a smart adjustment for us to not be going three days in a row of practice.” So far, the pivot from 3-day blocks hasn’t changed the 49ers’ injury luck. Multiple starters and contributors have already been dinged up, including Ricky Pearsall, Jordan James, and Malik Mustapha. The Niners can’t let the results frustrate their process. With some first-stringers out, that gives some of the depth an opportunity to fill in. Kubiak mentioned how that’s another benefit: “The other benefit of that was that everybody gets to practice every day. We have days when we were doing our traditional three-day block where a lot of vets would be missing that third day to kind of take the workload off of them. The way we’re doing it now is everyone’s out there every day and we don’t have to compensate for a lower number in a practice, which is where sometimes you might get an injury. When you’re low on receivers, one day you’re low on linemen or something, guys have to take more reps. So, we’re trying to avoid that as best we can by adding that jog-through day. Yesterday was good. It was our first one and hopefully we get the results we want moving forward.” More reps allows for the coaching staff to evaluate the youth and new faces on the roster. The 49ers don’t need to see what they have in a Christian McCaffrey, Fred Warner, or Trent Williams. We know Renardo Green is going to be a starting cornerback. But what if Jack Jones needs to play at some point? The same is true for Enrqiue Cruz Jr., Nick Martin, and a handful of other players up and down the roster.

title: Christian McCaffrey on 49ers rookie Kaelon Black: ‘I can’t say enough good things about him’

The 49ers headed into training camp hoping Black could be a part of a three-back stable alongside Christian McCaffrey and Jordan James. McCaffrey shared what he’s seen from Black early on in camp: “He’s stacked, man. You can definintely see it. He’s…you can tell he’s played at a high level of football. He’s played mature football. He’s again, he’s made..I can’t say enough good. He’s exactly what you would want a rookie to come in and be like. And again, I think our whole running back room is great, and he complements it so well in the way he runs. I think when you look at him, his rookie year, and then you go look at me, my rookie year, they look very different in age.” Black was born in 2001. Another running back on the roster, Sincere McCormick, was born in 2000. McCormick has been in the NFL since 2022. With James and Isaac Guerendo out, Black should get plenty of reps to show off his skill set. The only other running back on the roster outside of McCaffrey and McCormick is Patrick Taylor Jr., who might sneak onto the roster if James is out for an extended period. The 49ers should throw the kitchen sink at Black to see what he can and can’t handle in August. They’re going to need him early in the season to keep McCaffrey fresh for the duration of the season.

title: Baker Mayfield feels ‘disrespected’ by the Bucs
summary: Baker Mayfield didn’t hold back when discussing the failed contract negotiations with the Buccaneers following Thursday’s training camp practice. In fact, his frustration was evident on the topic. The veteran quarterback stated he felt “disrespected” and “undervalued” after extension talks stalled before camp. Mayfield talked about the deadline he set so his focus could shift […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - JULY 29: Baker Mayfield #6 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers takes the field during training camp at AdventHealth Training Center on July 29, 2026 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Mike Carlson/Getty Images) | Getty Images Baker Mayfield didn’t hold back when discussing the failed contract negotiations with the Buccaneers following Thursday’s training camp practice. In fact, his frustration was evident on the topic. The veteran quarterback stated he felt “disrespected” and “undervalued” after extension talks stalled before camp. Mayfield talked about the deadline he set so his focus could shift entirely to football, but believed the organization expected him to accept offers he felt didn’t reflect his value. “I wanted the deal done and set the deadline and told them it was going to be all ball after that, and I did mean that,” Mayfield said. “And I don’t know if they thought I was just going to take some of the offers that they gave, but I’m at the point of my career and understanding what I’ve brought to this franchise. One, I’m very, very thankful for the chance they gave me — do not get me wrong on that — but I also really know what I’ve brought to this franchise leadership-wise and even play-wise. It’s been some of the best years of my career, and I think it’s only going to trend upwards, just being comfortable and feeling that. So, disappointing in that regard to not have… to feel disrespected a little bit. And that’s really the disappointing part, to feel undervalued after thinking you’ve earned it.” Reports throughout negotiations indicated the two sides remained significantly apart, with Tampa Bay reportedly below Mayfield’s desired $50 million annual average value. Other reports also suggested the guarantees in the Buccaneers’ proposals were comparatively low, becoming another major sticking point in discussions. And all that is ‘too bad’ according to Mayfield. “If you’ve waited this long to take care of your franchise quarterback, that’s too bad because it’s only going to get worse from here. I’m going to have a really big year.” Mayfield noted, when speaking to ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler , the most disappointing part of the negotiations was that no offer had more than two years on it. Perhaps the Bucs played their cards right here. Mayfield had career numbers when he was slinging the ball around while Mike Evans was on the field. Now with Mike Evans gone, the team may want to see what he does now post-Evans. On the flip side, Tampa Bay’s signal caller believes he brings more to the table and even without Evans in the lineup — but having 2025 rookie receiver Emeka Egbuka — he was leading a lot of MVP talks at least through the midway point of last season. We may not know who took the right approach here until the season ends. The one thing that is certain here is that one side may be kicking themselves when it’s all said and done.

title: How Terry McLaurin has made a profound impact early in Commanders camp
summary: Terry McLaurin spoke to the media for 14 minutes and 55 seconds on Thursday afternoon, following the second Commanders training camp practice.   The veteran receiver talked about a ton, from Antonio Williams to Chig Okonkwo to his working relationship with quarterback Jayden Daniels and coordinator David Blough. Each answer was thoughtful and provided insight […]
full_text: Terry McLaurin spoke to the media for 14 minutes and 55 seconds on Thursday afternoon, following the second Commanders training camp practice. The veteran receiver talked about a ton, from Antonio Williams to Chig Okonkwo to his working relationship with quarterback Jayden Daniels and coordinator David Blough. Each answer was thoughtful and provided insight to the topic at hand. He was comfortable discussing the technical aspects of his position and how small adjustments can turn a small gain to big ones. There was one sentence among hundreds uttered that truly encapsulated McLaurin and his value to the 2026 Commanders. “I’m trying to think of things that help us all.” That line got me. McLaurin was talking specifically about the collaborative culture Blough is building, but it could’ve applied to any topic on the table. That seems to be McLaurin’s baseline motivation this year. I’m trying to think of things that help us all. That obviously involves his role as No. 1 receiver and a primary offensive producer. It involves his mentorship of young receivers. It involves making plays in practice that creates energy. It involves a conceptual knowledge of Blough’s offense and how best to function from each position, while understanding how he impacts those around him. It involves consistent work with Daniels throughout the offseason, and using the rapport built in previous seasons to adapt to and execute a new system. McLaurin wasn’t as involved to this point last season while working through a contract issue – he can’t be blamed for being a businessman – that ended in a three-year, $97 million contract extension . His impact has been felt this spring summer, in a massive and all-encompassing way. “His presence, his voice – this is a guy who has been doing it for countless years,” Daniels said on Wednesday. “…He’s a true pro, a true vet. You guys see him after practice, coaching up the younger guys and giving the game back his knowledge and energy.” That’s clear in McLaurin’s work with undrafted rookie Jaden Bradley . McLaurin is regularly seen pouring into the UNLV product after practice. This isn’t McLaurin’s first protege. He values the impact of giving back and was passionate about why he takes the time to do so. Terry McLaurin seemed to take undrafted rookie Jaden Bradley (among others) under his wing during OTAs and minicamp and has continued it into training camp. They were working together after practice today. pic.twitter.com/5SGr07wDnV — Nicki Jhabvala (@NickiJhabvala) July 29, 2026 “Since I’ve been here and got more years under my belt, I’ve always tried to bring young guys under my wing,” McLaurin said in his presser . “The great thing about it is that I’ve had young guys who are curious. I’m an open book. As a young guy, I was very curious and I had really good vets. I know the importance of passing that information. All of them have a great skill set or they wouldn’t be here. But there are nuances of the position. There’s gaining trust from the quarterback that’s very important. Creating certain habits at this level are important to establish the consistency that allows you to excel, continue to get better and have a long career. “It’s great to have a group of young guys who are hungry and looking to make the most of their opportunities. I’m happy to help them, but I learn something as well. …That’s a big part of being a leader. In camp, you see things from start to finish, see guys grow and see yourself grow and help build it from the ground up.” That was a long quote, but speaks directly to our overall theme. I’m trying to think of things that help us all. That motivation is clear in his work with Daniels, even on practice plays that work. The pair huddled up on Thursday after a successful completion and diagnosed how a productive play could’ve been better. McLaurin felt like he had to throttle a bit on the route to make the timing work. Was the issue Daniels’ eyes? Was it McLaurin’s steps within the route? They settled on McLaurin being just off on his split. Being right in that detail would’ve made all the difference. “With Jayden’s timing and our ability to run after catch, those can be huge plays,” McLaurin said. “That’s the difference between catch-and-tackle and catch-and-runs. We want catch-and-runs.” That comes with rapport between receiver and quarterback while working to execute a new offense. “We just communicate on and off the field a whole lot, whether it’s sitting in clips or talking to Blough about what we like,” McLaurin siad. “As long as we’re on the same page…When you’re on the same page with the quarterback, you can make any play right. That was the biggest thing for us, was getting reps and being on the same page. Now, as we incorporate this new offense, we’re trying to learn our assignments so we know our job first before focusing on the little nuances. “… It’s the details like that, being able to work on them so early, plus the years spent working together that will help us have a good season together.”
author: Scott Bair

title: Commanders injury news: Nick Allegretti, Treylon Burks banged up
summary: Commanders center Nick Allegretti suffered a calf strain on Wednesday, which caused him to leave training camp’s first practice early and with a trainer.   Head coach Dan Quinn updated Allegretti’s status before Thursday’s morning practice session, revealing the nature of his ailment. It is not expected to be a long-term issue.   “We’re still […]
full_text: Commanders center Nick Allegretti suffered a calf strain on Wednesday, which caused him to leave training camp’s first practice early and with a trainer. Head coach Dan Quinn updated Allegretti’s status before Thursday’s morning practice session, revealing the nature of his ailment. It is not expected to be a long-term issue. “We’re still going through the evaluation process,” Quinn said in a morning press conference . “(It’s) not something we’re overly concerned about in terms of a long (-term) deal), but I think I’ll know a little bit more through the weekend.” The Commanders have a scheduled off day on Friday, which will give Allegretti another chance to rest. Quinn also said that receiver Treylon Burks is dealing with some foot soreness that would keep him out of practice on Thursday. Burks’ foot situation is not considered long-term, but his troubling injury history magnifies even minor moments like these. Burks had a solid first day, highlighted by this touchdown catch in the red zone. Jayden Daniels to Treylon Burks for 6️⃣! pic.twitter.com/isOo54WCQE — brandon (@JayDanielsMVP) July 29, 2026 On-site reporters chronicled the fact that Julian Good-Jones was working with first-team quarterback Jayden Daniels in the early going. Jayden Daniels working with Julian Good-Jones during the early portion of camp today since Nick Allegretti (calf) is out. pic.twitter.com/1pehC0QUEa — Nicki Jhabvala (@NickiJhabvala) July 30, 2026 Sixth-round interior offensive lineman Matt Gulbin should also get a longer look with better units while Allegretti is out, which can be of benefit to a young player during training camp’s early stage. Same goes for Good-Jones, who might not get tons of reps with Daniels. “We just keep it going. Those are the (situations) were you move it around some,” Quinn said. “But, even within a practice, there are going to be times where a guys go up to the first group. Every player deserves a chance to go perform. “…We have about four guys who can snaps, so we rotate that through.”

Commanders links 🤝 pic.twitter.com/FhO2NMr8eZ — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) July 29, 2026 Articles The Athletic (paywall) How Daronte Jones, NFL ‘Renaissance Man,’ finally returned home with the Commanders Daronte Jones’ 14th move took him from Minneapolis, where he was the defensive backs coach of the Minnesota Vikings, to suburban Washington, where he is now the defensive coordinator of the Commanders. His new home field, Northwest Stadium, is around the corner from the elementary and middle schools where he first played football. He and his wife moved to McLean, Va., a short drive to the Commanders’ training facility in Ashburn. “Details kind of separate you from being average and being really good,” said Ken Norton Jr., the Commanders’ veteran linebackers coach who is working with Jones for the first time. “And he knows his details. He understands that we need to understand what the details are of each and every position and each and every coverage.” For Jones, that comes from a lifetime in coaching, from the countless mentors and peers who have provided lessons along the way. Over the phone, Brian Flores, the well-respected defensive coordinator of the Vikings, ticked off the virtues and talents of Daronte Jones, his former defensive backs coach. He’s creative, not afraid to test the limits, has a great way of relating to players — all the stuff you’d expect a boss to say when extolling the virtues of an understudy who advanced. Then he landed on a greater truth. “We call him the Renaissance Man,” Flores said. The Renaissance Man? “I mean, he’s the best-dressed guy in the building,” Flores said. “He’s got the best bags and luggage. He’s the most traveled. He has been all over the world.” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Heavy.com Jacory Croskey-Merritt has made a big change this offseason [John Keim] explained how Jacory Croskey-Merritt, ‘Bill’ said that he has added about seven to eight pounds of muscle. He looked bigger.” Keim also found out the reasoning behind Croskey-Merritt adding to his frame: “I asked him why he wanted to do? Well, it’s simple. He wants to break more tackles, and he can become the dynamic runner they need.” Making the most of Blough’s schemes will require Croskey-Merritt getting more from each carry, so it makes sense for him to bulk up, particularly when last year’s seventh-round pick only broke a tackle every 13.5 rushing attempts as a rookie, according to Pro Football Reference . A struggle keeping runs going after initial contact is one reason why the Croskey-Merritt struggled to earn enough carries in too many games. The more pressing adjustment for Croskey-Merrit involves ball security. He put the ball on the ground four times in 2025, so a change in mechanics is needed. Unfortunately, Keim noticed JCM “did have one run today which really nice run but at times you see that ball kind of extending from his body a little bit and so you want to make sure he’s taking care of the ball.” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE ESPN 2026 Washington Commanders training camp: Latest intel, updates Tuesday, July 28 With Tress Way sidelined by a pectoral injury, the Commanders signed veteran punter Matt Haack. Way, signed in 2015, is Washington’s longest-tenured player and signed a one-year deal this offseason. Peters said cornerback Trey Amos, who fractured his fibula in November, had some “soft-tissue issues” in the offseason was placed on the physically unable to perform list as a precautionary measure. Peters said Amos should return soon. Wednesday, July 29 Receiver Terry McLaurin has continued working with young wideouts after practice, as he did in the spring. He was giving tips to rookie receiver Jaden Bradley and second-year receiver Jacoby Jones. Both are facing tough battles just to make the roster. But McLaurin spent time with them after practice, covering them and giving them tips on how to handle certain coverages. Quinn said defensive end Dorance Armstrong, who tore his ACL in Week 6 last season, is “super close” to returning. Armstrong opened camp on the physically unable to perform list. Nick Allegretti, the favorite to start at center, left practice early for an undisclosed reason. He’s battling Julian Good-Jones for the starting job. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders.com Rasul Douglas wants to ‘be ready’ for any opportunity he gets in Commanders’ defense Rasul Douglas doesn’t know much about his situation with the Washington Commanders yet. Wednesday was his first day with the team, so he doesn’t know much about his teammates aside from those he has either trained with — Antonio Hamilton Sr. and Nick Cross — or played with at a previous stop like Amik Robertson. He’s never played for Daronte Jones before, so he’s still learning the new system. Here’s what he does know, though: he wants to be part of what the Commanders are building, and he wants to add something the defense struggled to get in 2025. “Turnovers,” Douglas said. “That’s what I do. I get turnovers.” He’s listed as 6-foot-2 and 209 pounds, which makes him the biggest cornerback on the roster. The Commanders like their options in Robertson and Mike Sainristil, but Douglas has the size and length to hang with bigger receivers on the perimeter. Douglas is now one of the most experienced players in the cornerback room. He’s played in 135 games for five teams spread across nine seasons. He’s also been a starter more often than not in his career, and was most recently a fixture of the Miami Dolphins’ defense. He started 13 games in 2025, recording 62 tackles and two interceptions in that span. All that’s to say, Douglas is used to being in unfamiliar situations. He’s worked in several defensive schemes over the years, and one thing he has learned is that players coming into new situations need to “be ready” for anything. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE JP Finlay Training Camp Day 1: Good day for WRs [I]f they keep saying they like the current group – even if Peters allowed the organization is always looking to get better at every position – maybe we should believe them? Training Camp Day 1 was a good day for the believe them crowd. Dyami Brown and Treylon Burks both made toe tap touchdown grabs on contested catches. Rookie Antonio Williams repeatedly made impressive grabs, showing quickness and speed, which are different. It’s too early to be too excited about any of the receivers not named McLaurin, but in a primarily red zone practice, the receiver group answered the bell. Williams in particular made a move on Commanders LB Leo Chenal that looked close to unstoppable. The question for Williams will be what happens when the pads come on. The slippery rook has impressed, but let’s see him do it facing press coverage against a long-armed NFL corner like Amik Robertson , or when the threat of a shoulder pop from Chenal impacts the possible movement in the open field. It was just one day, but it was a good one for the receiving group. (That still doesn’t preclude Adam Peters from signing another vet.)
